sermon:
## The Power of God for Salvation: Not Ashamed of the Gospel (Romans 1:1-17)
*What Paul stakes his whole life on before he argues a single point*

**Text:** Romans 1:1-17 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 52:7 · Habakkuk 2:4 · Psalm 98:2 · 2 Timothy 1:8 · Mark 8:38

Paul had never been to Rome. He wrote to a church he did not plant, in a city he did not know, at the center of an empire that would one day kill him for the very message this letter carries. And before he corrects a single error, before he settles a single dispute, he tells them what he is not. He is not ashamed. In a culture that had already decided a crucified Jewish carpenter was an embarrassment — and ours has decided the same — the first thing the apostle establishes is not a defense but a confession. Not "here is why the gospel is respectable." Not "here is how we make it palatable." He plants his flag on the one thing the world calls foolish and says: this is where I stand, and I am not embarrassed to stand here.

We live at the far end of Christendom now, and we have inherited its instinct to apologize. We soften. We qualify. We reach for the version of the message that will keep the room, and we tell ourselves that keeping the room is the same thing as loving it. Paul had no such instinct, and he had far more reason for one than we do. Rome could kill him for this letter, and eventually would. Watch, then, what he does before he ever mentions being unashamed. He does not build a case for his own credibility. He builds a case for the gospel's ancientness, its royalty, and its power — and only then does he say the word that has echoed down twenty centuries.

### I. The Gospel Was Promised Before It Arrived (Romans 1:1-4)

Paul does not open by introducing himself as clever. He opens by naming himself owned. "Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God" (Romans 1:1). The word behind *servant* is *doulos* — slave, bondservant, a man whose life is not his own. He begins with his own smallness so the gospel can be large.

And then he says the thing the modern reader rushes past. This gospel was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures" (Romans 1:2). It did not begin at Bethlehem. It did not begin when a voice was needed to answer the emptiness of the age. It began in the mind of God and was announced through centuries of prophets who died without seeing it. The gospel is not new. It is the oldest thing there is, breaking into time.

Concerning his Son, "who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 1:3-4). Flesh and Spirit. Son of David and Son of God. Born and raised. The whole gospel is compressed into two verses before the letter properly begins. And the last three words carry a charge the Roman reader would have felt in the body: *Jesus Christ our Lord*. In an empire where Caesar was *Kyrios*, lord, to name a crucified Galilean as Lord was not a devotional flourish. It was a rival throne. Paul opens with a confession that could get a man executed, and he opens with it as though it were the most settled fact in the world.

This is why the gospel is not fragile. It is not a recent idea competing for a hearing among newer ideas. It is the oldest promise there is, sworn by God, carried by prophets, fulfilled in a King raised from the dead. A man ashamed of a fashion apologizes when the fashion turns. A man standing on something ancient and true has nothing to apologize for.

- **A. The full historical arc** — Paul refuses to start at the proximate cause. The gospel reaches back through David, through the prophets, through the covenant. A faith with no roots blows away in the first wind; Paul plants his in the deepest soil there is.
- **B. Declared, not achieved** — Jesus was *declared* Son of God in power by the resurrection. The empty tomb is not a happy postscript. It is God's public verdict on his Son, and Paul builds everything on it.

### II. The Righteousness of God Revealed From Faith to Faith (Romans 1:5-17)

Paul longs to come to Rome — not to be entertained, not to be admired, but "that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you" and "that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith" (Romans 1:11-12). Even an apostle needs the church. He does not arrive as the expert who has it all and dispenses to those who have none. He comes to give and to receive. That is what a servant does.

Then comes the hinge of the whole letter. "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith'" (Romans 1:16-17).

Notice what the power is. Paul does not say the gospel *points to* the power of God. He says the gospel *is* the power of God — *dynamis*, the word underneath our word dynamite, though it means far more than an explosion. It means effective, working, saving power. The message itself does the thing. When Isaiah wrote, "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news" (Isaiah 52:7), he understood that the announcement is not decoration on the rescue. The announcement is how the rescue arrives.

And the phrase Paul reaches for last is the phrase everything hangs on: *the righteousness of God*. Not our righteousness offered up to God. The righteousness that belongs to God, revealed and given away in the gospel. Habakkuk said it seven centuries before Paul: "the righteous shall live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). Paul takes that one line and builds sixteen chapters on it. And the psalmist had already tied the two threads together — righteousness and salvation, God's own and freely shown: "The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations" (Psalm 98:2). What was revealed to the prophets in fragments is now revealed in full, in a Person, from faith for faith.

Read that last phrase slowly, because it is easy to skip and impossible to overstate. *From faith for faith.* There is no other entry point. Not from effort for reward. Not from lineage for privilege. Faith at the door and faith all the way through. The righteousness is God's from beginning to end, and the only hand that receives it is the empty one.

- **A. Power, not advice** — The gospel is not a technique for self-improvement. It is the power of God for salvation. If it has become in our mouths a set of tips for a better life, we have traded dynamite for a matchbook.
- **B. To the Jew first and also to the Greek** — The gospel breaks every wall it touches. It humbles the insider and welcomes the outsider on identical terms: faith, and nothing else.

### III. Living Unashamed in a Post-Christian Culture

Here is where the mirror turns, and it turns on us. We are the church at the far end of the West's long turning away, and we have made a quiet peace with shame. We do not deny the gospel. We soften it. We lead with our relevance and mention the cross late, apologetically, hoping it will not cost us the room. I have done this from a pulpit — reached for the acceptable angle, buried the offense of the cross under a paragraph of throat-clearing, and called my cowardice wisdom.

Consider what Paul was up against. When he wrote *the righteous shall live by faith*, that same line had already been carried by Habakkuk across the fall of a nation, and in the sixteenth century a monk named Martin Luther, terrified of the righteousness of God because he thought it meant only the standard that condemned him, read Romans 1:17 and understood at last that this righteousness is *given*, not demanded. It broke him open. He wrote that he felt himself "to be reborn and to have gone through open doors into paradise." The whole Reformation turns on one preposition in one verse: the righteousness of God, revealed *from* faith *for* faith. Luther was not ashamed either. It cost him everything, and he was not ashamed.

Jesus said, "whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father" (Mark 8:38). That is not a threat handed to enemies. It is a warning handed to the church. The generation Paul feared and the generation Luther feared and the generation you and I live in all share one temperament: they are embarrassed by the cross. And the only cure Paul knows is not better marketing. It is the gospel itself, which is the power of God, doing what no marketing can do — raising the dead.

Paul told Timothy the same thing at the end, when the sword was near: "do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God" (2 Timothy 1:8). Notice that even there, the antidote to shame is the same word from Romans 1 — *power*. Shame is cured not by manufacturing courage but by knowing what you are holding. A man ashamed of the gospel has, at some level, forgotten that it is loaded.

So the question this text leaves is not whether the gospel is respectable enough for our moment. It never was respectable, in any moment. The question is whether we still believe it is the power of God — because a man who believes he is holding the power of God to raise the dead does not apologize for it in a room full of the dying.

- **A. We did not fall by denial** — We fell by embarrassment. The church in the West did not mostly abandon the gospel; it apologized for it until the apology replaced it.
- **B. Christ is the righteousness revealed** — The righteousness of God is not a quality you manufacture on your best morning. It is a Person, credited to you the moment you believe. To be joined to him is to be counted righteous. That is why Paul can face Rome and death and shame with the same sentence: I am not ashamed.

The gospel itself is the power.

## The Wrath of God Revealed: Suppressing the Truth We Already Know (Romans 1:18-32)
*Why the problem is not ignorance but a truth held down by force*

**Text:** Romans 1:18-32 · **Supporting:** Psalm 19:1 · Romans 2:15 · Jeremiah 2:13 · John 3:19 · Ephesians 4:18

Paul has just told us the gospel is the power of God for salvation. Now he tells us why anyone would need saving at all. And he does not begin where we expect. He does not begin with the obvious sinner, the one everyone agrees is far gone. He begins with the wrath of God, revealed already, right now, against a race of people who know better than they live. The diagnosis before the cure. You cannot understand the good news of chapter three until you have felt the weight of the bad news here.

We flinch at the word *wrath*. We would rather have a God who is only patient. But Paul writes plainly, and the plain word is the true one.

### I. The Wrath Already Revealed Against Suppressed Truth (Romans 1:18-23)

"For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (Romans 1:18). Note the tense. Not *will be* revealed at the end of history — though it will. It *is* revealed, present tense, already at work. And note the word *suppress*. The Greek is *katechō*, to hold down, to press down, to restrain by force. Paul is not describing people who never heard. He is describing people who heard, and pushed the truth underwater, and held it there.

Because the truth was available. "For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse" (Romans 1:19-20). The psalmist said it first: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork" (Psalm 19:1). The evidence is not hidden. It is everywhere. The problem was never a shortage of light.

The problem is what we did with it. "For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened" (Romans 1:21). This is the great exchange. "They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things" (Romans 1:23). Jeremiah named the same crime centuries before: "they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13). We do not lose the truth by accident. We trade it. We swap the glory of God for something we can manage.

And note the order Paul gives, because it is the order of every fall. First they refused to honor and to thank; then their thinking went futile; then the heart went dark; then the idols came. The idol is never the first move. It is the last symptom of a first refusal. Paul writes elsewhere of a mind "darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). The hardness comes first. The darkness follows the hardness. The refusal to give thanks is where the whole ruin begins — not in a laboratory of doubt, but in a heart that will not bow.

- **A. Without excuse** — Paul closes the door on the alibi we most want to keep. Nobody stands before God pleading they never knew. The knowledge was there. The suppression was ours.
- **B. The exchange is the sin under the sins** — Every particular wrong Paul is about to list grows from this one root: we swapped the Creator for the creature. Name that, and the rest follows.

### II. God Handed Them Over to What They Chose (Romans 1:24-32)

Three times Paul says the same terrible thing. "Therefore God gave them up" (Romans 1:24). "For this reason God gave them up" (Romans 1:26). "And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind" (Romans 1:28). The verb is *paradidōmi* — to hand over, to deliver up. It is the same verb used when Jesus is handed over to be crucified. Here is the wrath already revealed, and it is more frightening than fire. God's judgment, in this age, is often that he lets us have exactly what we insisted on.

We imagine wrath as God intervening. Paul shows us a wrath that is God *withdrawing* — removing the restraint, releasing us to the desires we demanded the freedom to pursue. "God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves" (Romans 1:24). The cage door opens, and the punishment is that we are free to run where we always wanted to run, and to discover it was a cliff. This is a grief, not a taunt. There is nothing in Paul's tone here of a man enjoying the ruin of his enemies. There is the ache of a physician naming a terminal disease he cannot pretend away, because pretending would be the crueler thing.

And it should sober us that the mechanism of judgment is desire itself. A generation raised to believe that following your desires is the whole meaning of freedom has no defense against a God whose wrath, in part, is simply to say yes. To be handed over to your appetites is not liberation. It is a sentence carried out under the disguise of a permission. The most frightening thing God can do to a hardened people is not to strike them. It is to leave them alone. To stop resisting them. To let them have, without interruption, exactly the life they demanded — and to let the getting of it be the punishment.

Then Paul lists it — the whole catalog of a humanity unmoored, "filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice... envy, murder, strife, deceit... gossips, slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful" (Romans 1:29-30). And it is a mercy that gossip and pride sit in the same sentence as murder, because it means none of us gets to read this list as being about someone else. The catalog is a mirror. Jesus said it plainly: "the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil" (John 3:19). Not could not see. Loved the dark.

- **A. Wrath as abandonment** — The most terrifying judgment in this chapter is not God striking. It is God stepping back. To be handed over to yourself is a sentence.
- **B. They know and approve** — Paul ends by saying they "know God's righteous decree" yet "give approval to those who practice" evil (Romans 1:32). The conscience is not dead. It is overruled, and cheered against.

### III. The Suppressed Truth in a Post-Christian Culture

Turn the mirror. It has been describing the ancient pagan the whole time, and we have nodded along, because we had someone in mind. Turn around. Paul's word *suppress* is not a museum piece. It is the machinery of the modern heart, and it is the machinery of mine. I have known things about God and about myself at three in the morning that I spent the daylight hours holding under. I have called my fear discernment and my appetite freedom, and I have done it from a pulpit. The suppression Paul describes is not something the enlightened West outgrew. It is the West's operating system.

The historian is worth hearing here. In his 2019 book *Dominion*, Tom Holland, no apologist for the church, argues that the moral instincts the modern West is most proud of — its horror at cruelty, its insistence on the dignity of the weak, its very idea that conscience matters — did not spring from Greece or Rome, which had no such instincts, but from the long saturation of Europe in Christian belief. Holland set out to write as a secular man and found, to his own discomfort, that his own moral reflexes were Christian to the root. The Roman world he admired felt cruelty and inequality to be simply the order of things; the notion that the weak have a claim on the strong is a specifically Christian intrusion into history. Holland's point cuts exactly where Paul's does: our culture goes on eating the fruit of a tree it has decided to cut down. It keeps the ethics and suppresses the source. It keeps the conscience Paul says God wrote on the heart (Romans 2:15) and denies the God who wrote it. That is *katechō* on a civilizational scale — the truth held down, and the branch we are standing on sawn behind us.

But here is why the diagnosis is mercy and not despair. The same Christ who was *handed over* — *paradidōmi*, the very word for the wrath in this chapter — was handed over for us. Watch the verb move. In Romans 1, God hands sinners over to their sin. In the Gospels, God hands his own Son over to the cross. Paul will say it plainly a few chapters on: God "did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all" (Romans 8:32) — gave him up, *paradidōmi*, the same word. The wrath we suppressed our way into fell, in full, on the One who never suppressed a thing. God gave us up to our sin; then God gave up his own Son to that same wrath in our place. The verdict of this chapter is real, and it lands on all of us, and the only door out of it is the One who walked through the wrath we earned.

That is why a chapter this dark can be preached at all. Romans 1 is not written to make us despair of ourselves and stop there. It is written to end our self-defense so completely that when the cross is named, we have nothing left to say but yes. The suppression has to be exposed before the mercy can be received. A man who still thinks he is fine has no use for a Savior. Romans 1 takes the fine away.

- **A. We are not the exception** — Every reader wants this chapter to be about the culture out there. It is about the heart in here. We knew, and we held it down.
- **B. The handed-over Son** — The wrath we suppressed our way into, Christ absorbed. That is the only reason a chapter this dark can be preached as good news at all.

We knew, and we suppressed it.

## No One Is Righteous: How Every Mouth Is Stopped Before God (Romans 2:1-3:20)
*Why the moral person is in as much danger as the immoral one*

**Text:** Romans 2:1-3:20 · **Supporting:** Psalm 143:2 · Psalm 14:1-3 · Matthew 7:1-2 · 1 Samuel 16:7 · Galatians 2:16

Paul has just finished the list. The lusts, the malice, the gossips and the murderers, humanity handed over to itself. And there is a person reading who has been enjoying every word — the decent, upright, religious person who agrees the world is a mess and is quietly certain the mess is other people. Paul turns to that person now. He turns to me. Because the trap of chapter one is not that it condemns the obvious sinner. The trap is that it sets up the respectable one to feel safe. And Paul springs it in the very first verse of chapter two.

This is the longest step in Paul's argument, and the hardest to survive, because it takes away the last place we hide: our comparative goodness.

### I. The One Who Judges Condemns Himself (Romans 2:1-16)

"Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things" (Romans 2:1). The finger that pointed through all of chapter one now curls back. The moment you condemn, you convict yourself, because you know the standard well enough to apply it — which means you know it well enough to be measured by it.

Jesus said the identical thing on a hillside: "Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you" (Matthew 7:1-2). Paul is not forbidding all moral discernment. He is exposing the man who uses the ruler on his neighbor and hides it when it comes to himself. The very sharpness of your eye for another's fault is the proof you own the standard — and owning the standard is exactly what condemns you when you fail it. The clearer your sight of sin in someone else, the fewer excuses you have for your own.

And Paul warns that God's patience is not God's approval. "Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?" (Romans 2:4). The delay of judgment is mercy, not indifference — a door held open, not a case dismissed. To read God's patience as permission is to store up wrath "for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5). The kindest thing God does — waiting — is the thing the presumptuous heart most abuses.

And Paul strips away the two things the religious insider trusts most. First, heritage does not save. "For God shows no partiality" (Romans 2:11). Second, and more devastating for a Jew: circumcision does not save. "For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit" (Romans 2:28-29). The badge of belonging saves no one. God has never once, in the whole history of the world, been impressed by a badge.

- **A. Knowing the law is not keeping the law** — Paul says it is "not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified" (Romans 2:13). Possession of the truth condemns you faster if you do not live it.
- **B. God sees the heart** — The Lord told Samuel, "man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Every hidden thing is his witness. There is no outward performance that survives that gaze.

### II. Both Jew and Gentile Stand Under Sin (Romans 3:1-20)

Paul lets the objection speak. "Then what advantage has the Jew?" (Romans 3:1). He grants it — "Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God" (Romans 3:2). Real privilege, real trust. But privilege is not acquittal. Paul presses to the verdict he has been building toward since chapter one. "What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin" (Romans 3:9).

Then he does what a prophet does. He indicts with Scripture, stacking the witnesses. "None is righteous, no, one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one" (Romans 3:10-12). He is quoting the Psalms — "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'... they have all turned aside... there is none who does good, not even one" (Psalm 14:1-3). The whole race, one verdict, no exceptions.

And Paul tells us what the law was for all along. "Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God" (Romans 3:19). Every mouth stopped. The Greek word Paul uses, *phrassō*, is the word for stopping up, blocking, fencing shut. It pictures a courtroom where the accused, given every chance to speak in his own defense, finally has nothing to say — the alibis exhausted, the character witnesses spent, the mouth that never stops defending itself at last shut. Then the last word: "For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin" (Romans 3:20). The law was never the ladder. It was the mirror. It was never meant to lift us up. It was meant to show us we cannot climb.

Paul says the same thing to the Galatians, and it is worth setting beside this verse: "we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ... because by works of the law no one will be justified" (Galatians 2:16). Twice in one sentence he closes the door on the law as a means of acquittal. The law is holy and good and does exactly what it was designed to do — and what it was designed to do is not to save you but to strip you of the illusion that you could save yourself.

- **A. The law diagnoses, it does not cure** — "Through the law comes knowledge of sin." A mirror shows you the dirt; it was never going to wash your face.
- **B. Every mouth stopped** — This is the goal of the whole section. Not most mouths. Every one. The self-defense finally runs out, and the silence is where grace can finally be heard.

### III. The Stopped Mouth in a Post-Christian Culture

Turn the mirror one more time, because Paul has built this entire section to turn it on the last person standing — the good one. And in our moment, the good one is not usually the churchgoer boasting in his righteousness. He is the decent secular person, morally serious, certain he is on the right side, measuring the world by a standard he assumes he himself has met. I know him because I am him. I have stood over other people's sins with a ruler and kept the ruler in my pocket when the sin was mine. That is the exact posture Romans 2:1 destroys, and it destroys it in the pew and the pulpit as fast as anywhere.

Here the moral psychologist helps us see the machinery. Jonathan Haidt, in his 2012 book *The Righteous Mind*, argues from years of research that human moral reasoning does not work the way we think. We do not weigh the evidence and then reach a verdict. We reach the verdict first — instantly, intuitively, in favor of ourselves — and then our reasoning runs behind like a press secretary, inventing justifications for a conclusion already decided. Haidt calls the reasoning mind the rider on an elephant, and the rider mostly serves the elephant. That is Romans 3 in a laboratory. We are not neutral judges who occasionally err. We are advocates for ourselves who were never going to rule against the client. Which is precisely why Paul says the mouth must be *stopped*. The self-defense will never end on its own. It has to be silenced from outside.

Haidt is a working psychologist writing without any theological interest, describing what he found in the data — and what he found is the doctrine of Romans 3 rendered in the language of the laboratory. We are not truth-seekers who occasionally rationalize. We are rationalizers who occasionally stumble onto truth. The mouth defends the self by design, not by accident. Which is why Paul does not say the mouth is persuaded, or corrected, or improved. He says it is *stopped*. Persuasion works on a fair judge. The self is not a fair judge of the self, and never was.

David knew this a thousand years before Paul quoted him. "Enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you" (Psalm 143:2). David does not ask God to weigh him fairly. He knows what a fair weighing costs. He asks God not to enter into judgment at all — because the only hope of the guilty is not a fair trial but a merciful one.

And that stopped mouth is not the end. It is the doorway. Paul spends two and a half chapters closing every other door precisely so that when he says "But now" in the next breath, we have nowhere else to run except to the righteousness of God given in Christ. The law stops your mouth so the gospel can open it again — this time in praise. There is a real mercy in being brought to the end of your excuses, though it never feels like mercy while it is happening. Every alibi God takes from you is a false hope he is prying loose so your hand is empty enough to receive the true one. The most dangerous position a person can hold before God is not open sin. It is the quiet confidence of the decent man who has never once been silenced.

- **A. Moral seriousness is not innocence** — The person most sure he has met the standard is the person Paul most needs to reach. Being right about the world's evil is not the same as being clean of it.
- **B. The silence points to the cross** — Every mouth stopped is not God's cruelty. It is God clearing the room of excuses so the only remaining word is the name of his Son.

No one is righteous, not one.

## Justified Freely by His Grace: But Now a Righteousness From God (Romans 3:21-31)
*The two words that turn the whole letter, and the cross that makes God both just and justifier*

**Text:** Romans 3:21-31 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:5-6 · Leviticus 16:15-16 · 2 Corinthians 5:21 · Ephesians 2:8-9 · 1 John 2:2

For three chapters Paul has been closing doors. The pagan without excuse, the moralist condemned by his own ruler, the religious insider whose badge saves no one, every mouth stopped and the whole world held accountable to God. If you have felt the weight of the first three chapters, you are standing exactly where Paul wants you — with nothing left to say and nowhere left to run. And into that silence he speaks the two words that turn the entire letter, the two words the Reformation was fought over, the two words a guilty person waits a lifetime to hear.

"But now."

### I. A Righteousness From God, Apart From the Law (Romans 3:21-24)

"But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the law and the Prophets bear witness to it — the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe" (Romans 3:21-22). Everything hangs on that phrase, *apart from the law*. The righteousness we could never manufacture, the standard the mirror proved we could not reach, has been *manifested* — brought into the open, given — from outside the whole system of our performance. It does not come up from us. It comes down from God.

And it is for everyone, because the disease is universal. "For there is no distinction: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (Romans 3:22-24). Read that slowly, because two words in it carry the gospel. *Gift* — *dōrean*, freely, gratis, without payment. And *redemption* — *apolytrōsis*, the price paid to free a slave from the market. It is free to us because it was paid for by him. Grace is never cheap. It is free to the guilty precisely because it was ruinously expensive to God.

Hold those two words together, because our age constantly pulls them apart. It wants the gift without the redemption — grace as a general divine leniency, God overlooking sin because God is nice. Paul will not allow it. The gift is real and it is free, but it comes *through* a redemption, a purchase, a price. A gift that cost the giver nothing is not grace. It is indifference wearing grace's coat. The wonder of Romans 3 is not that God waved off the debt. It is that God paid it himself and then handed us the receipt for nothing.

- **A. Apart from the law** — This righteousness does not stand at the end of your effort as a reward. It stands apart from your effort as a gift. That is the offense of grace and its glory.
- **B. No distinction** — All have sinned; all are justified the same way. The gospel levels the ground completely. There is no fast lane for the respectable and no back door for the notorious. One door, and it is Christ.

### II. A Propitiation by His Blood, So God Is Just and Justifier (Romans 3:25-31)

Now Paul reaches for the deepest word in the chapter. God "put forward" Christ "as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith" (Romans 3:25). *Hilastērion* — propitiation. It is a sacrificial word, and it points back to the mercy seat, the lid over the ark where on the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkled the blood (Leviticus 16:15-16). It means the turning away of wrath. And this is where a soft gospel and the real one part ways. The wrath of Romans 1:18 was real. Sin against an infinite God is not waved off. It is *paid*. On the cross, the wrath we earned fell on the One who did not earn it.

Why did God do it this way? Paul tells us, and the answer is the beating heart of the letter. "It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). Hold both halves. God is *just* — he does not pretend our sin never happened; he judges it fully at the cross. And God is the *justifier* — he declares the guilty righteous. A judge who simply excuses evil is not good; he is corrupt. A judge who only condemns cannot save. At the cross, God does the impossible thing: he punishes the sin and pardons the sinner, because the sin was punished in his Son. Isaiah saw it seven centuries out: "he was pierced for our transgressions... and with his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray... and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:5-6).

Then Paul asks the question that follows. "Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded" (Romans 3:27). If salvation is a gift received by faith, there is nothing left to boast in. This is not a minor consequence; it is the whole point. A gospel of works always leaves a scrap of boasting intact, and that scrap is enough to feed the pride that damns. Grace does not leave the scrap. It takes the whole loaf, so that the mouth stopped in Romans 3:19 can only open again to praise, never to preen. "For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28). Paul the Jew even insists this makes God the God of Gentiles too, "since God is one" (Romans 3:29-30), and one God saves all people one way. He ends by anticipating the objection that grace destroys the law — "Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means. On the contrary, we uphold the law" (Romans 3:31) — because the cross does not cancel God's justice. It honors it to the last drop.

- **A. Propitiation, not mere example** — The cross is not chiefly a demonstration of love in the abstract. It is the place wrath was satisfied. Remove that, and Isaiah 53 makes no sense and Romans 1 has no answer.
- **B. Just and justifier** — This is the sentence the whole letter turns on. God did not lower the standard to save you. He met it himself, in his Son, so that mercy and justice kissed at the cross instead of colliding.

### III. The Great Exchange in a Post-Christian Culture

Turn it toward us, because the modern heart resists this chapter at exactly one point. We will accept a God of love. We recoil at a God of wrath and blood and propitiation. It sounds primitive to us, beneath the dignity of an enlightened age. And I have felt the pull to preach the love and quietly retire the wrath, to keep Romans 3:24 and lose Romans 3:25, to offer grace without ever explaining what it cost. That is not a kinder gospel. It is a smaller God and a cheaper cross. And it is a strange kind of arrogance to think ourselves too advanced for the blood, given what our advanced century actually produced. The same age that finds propitiation distasteful gave the world the trench and the camp and the bomb. We are in no position to lecture the cross about violence. We are in a position to be saved from ours.

Here the Reformation is not a footnote but the point. For most of his early life Martin Luther, an Augustinian monk, read the phrase *the righteousness of God* and hated it, because he could only hear it as the standard by which God would condemn him — a bar he could never clear, no matter how he fasted or confessed or scourged himself. He said he came to loathe the very word. Then, reading Romans, he grasped that the righteousness of God in the gospel is not the standard God demands but the gift God gives. When Luther came to *hilastērion* and to *justified by his grace as a gift*, he understood that the righteousness God requires, God supplies. The Reformers had a phrase for it — *iustitia aliena*, an alien righteousness, a righteousness from outside us, credited to our account. Paul says it in one unbearable, glorious line elsewhere: God "made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is the great exchange. My sin was reckoned to Christ; his righteousness is reckoned to me. Not earned. Not deserved. Received by faith, "by grace... through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Luther called the discovery of this an open door into paradise, and five centuries later the door has not closed.

There is a pastoral weight in this that the guilty conscience needs to feel. If your righteousness is your own, then your standing before God rises and falls with your worst week, and you will never once be sure of him. But if your righteousness is *alien* — Christ's, credited, held in heaven's ledger, not manufactured on your best morning — then your standing does not move when you fail, because it was never resting on you to begin with. The believer's assurance is not confidence in himself. It is confidence in a verdict already rendered over Someone else and reckoned to his account. That is why the doctrine that humbles most also comforts most.

So the question Romans 3 leaves is not whether you are good enough. That question was answered in chapter three, verse twenty, and the answer was no. The question is whether you will let your mouth stay stopped in your own defense long enough to hear the verdict already spoken over Christ. He is our propitiation, "and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2). The gavel has already come down. It came down on him.

- **A. We cannot edit the cross** — Cut the wrath and you cut the mercy, because mercy that costs nothing saves nothing. The blood is not the embarrassment of the gospel. It is the gospel.
- **B. His righteousness for our sin** — To be in Christ is to be counted righteous with a righteousness you did not produce. That is the only standing that survives Romans 1 through 3, and it is a free gift.

Just, and the one who justifies.

## Justified by Faith Alone: Abraham Believed God (Romans 4:1-25)
*Why Paul proves grace from the man every Jew called father*

**Text:** Romans 4:1-25 · **Supporting:** Genesis 15:6 · Genesis 17:5 · Psalm 32:1-2 · Galatians 3:6-9 · Hebrews 11:8-12

Paul has laid it down. Justified freely by grace, through faith, apart from works of the law. And he can hear the objection forming, because it is the oldest objection there is: *fine for the pagan, but surely not for Abraham.* Surely the father of the faithful, the man God chose, the man who left everything and offered his own son — surely he earned something. So Paul does the boldest thing he could do. He takes the objectors' greatest hero and proves grace from him. Not from a marginal figure. From Abraham. From the very man every Jew called father.

If grace holds for Abraham, it holds for anyone. Paul knows it, and he goes straight for the strongest case against him.

### I. Abraham Believed God, and It Was Counted to Him (Romans 4:1-8)

"What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God" (Romans 4:1-2). Paul grants the whole weight of the objection and then answers it not with his opinion but with Scripture. "For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness'" (Romans 4:3). He is quoting Genesis 15:6 — a verse written long before the law, long before circumcision, long before the temple. Abraham did not achieve righteousness. He *believed*, and God *counted* it to him.

That word *counted* is the hinge — *logizomai*, an accounting term, to reckon, to credit to an account. Paul presses the metaphor. "Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness" (Romans 4:4-5). Read the phrase that should stop us cold — God "justifies the ungodly." Not the godly. Not the deserving. The ungodly. If you work, you earn wages, and God owes you nothing but judgment. If you believe, you receive a gift, and God credits to you a righteousness you never worked for.

Paul brings a second witness, David, who "speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: 'Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin'" (Romans 4:6-8, quoting Psalm 32:1-2). Same word — *logizomai* again — but now Paul shows both sides of the ledger. God does not *count* the sin; God *counts* the righteousness. Two entries in the divine account, and both are grace. And notice which man David has in mind. David wrote Psalm 32 after his adultery and his arranged murder, from the far side of the worst thing he ever did. That is the blessed man — not the one with a clean record, but the one whose filthy record God refuses to count against him. Abraham the great believer and David the great sinner arrive at the same door, and it is the only door there is.

- **A. Counted, not earned** — Justification is God crediting to your account a righteousness that is not yours by works. The transaction happens in heaven's ledger, received by faith.
- **B. He justifies the ungodly** — This is the scandal the whole chapter guards. God does not wait for you to become worthy. He justifies the ungodly, or he justifies no one at all.

### II. The Father of All Who Believe (Romans 4:9-25)

Now Paul asks the decisive timing question. When was Abraham counted righteous — before or after circumcision? "How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised" (Romans 4:10). Genesis 15 comes years before Genesis 17. Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised, while still, by the later badge, an outsider. Therefore, Paul says, he is "the father of all who believe without being circumcised" as well as of the circumcised who "walk in the footsteps of the faith" (Romans 4:11-12). The order of the story preaches the gospel: grace first, then the sign; faith first, then the mark. Never the reverse.

And the promise never ran through law at all. "For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith" (Romans 4:13). If the inheritance came by law-keeping, faith would be pointless and the promise void (Romans 4:14). Grace runs on a different track entirely.

Then Paul shows us what Abraham's faith actually was — and it was not a vague optimism. It was trust in a specific kind of God. Abraham was "fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised" (Romans 4:21), and this against every visible fact: a hundred years old, his own body "as good as dead," Sarah's womb barren (Romans 4:19). "In hope he believed against hope" (Romans 4:18). God had renamed him — "I have made you the father of many nations" (Genesis 17:5, quoted in Romans 4:17) — before there was a single child. The writer of Hebrews saw the same faith: Abraham "went out, not knowing where he was going" (Hebrews 11:8). Faith is not certainty about circumstances. It is trust in the character of the God who "gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist" (Romans 4:17).

Then Paul closes the loop and pulls us into the story. This was written "not for his sake alone... but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification" (Romans 4:23-25).

- **A. Grace before the badge** — Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, so no ritual, no lineage, no ceremony is the ground of acceptance. Faith is, and faith alone.
- **B. The God who raises the dead** — Abraham trusted the God who brings life from a dead womb; we trust the God who brought his Son from a dead tomb. Same God, same faith, same crediting.

### III. Believing Against Hope in a Post-Christian Culture

Turn it on us. We are heirs of a culture that has been catechized to distrust the very thing Abraham was praised for. Our age treats faith as a failure of nerve, a refusal to face reality, the thing you resort to when the evidence runs out. And the church has half-swallowed the slander. We speak of faith as a feeling we work up, or a badge we display, or a lever we pull to get what we want from God. But Abraham's faith was none of that. It was the sane and stubborn conviction that the God who spoke could be trusted against every appearance — and I confess I trust my circumstances more than I trust him most mornings, which is exactly the inversion this chapter destroys.

Consider what Paul is doing historically, because it is stunning. He is standing inside first-century Judaism, arguing with the fiercest defenders of the law — men who could recite Abraham's obedience from memory and staked their standing before God on being his physical children — and he beats them at their own text. He does not smuggle grace in around Abraham; he plants it in Genesis 15, four centuries before Sinai, and dares anyone to move it. The chronology itself is his argument: righteousness credited in Genesis 15, circumcision commanded in Genesis 17, the law given at Sinai centuries later still. Grace was first. Grace was always first. In the 1500s, when the Reformers recovered *sola fide* — faith alone — they were not inventing something new. They were reading Romans 4 and refusing to look away. Luther and Calvin both understood that Paul's whole case against a religion of merit stands or falls on one Hebrew sentence about Abraham, and it does not fall. The man every merit-seeker claimed as father turns out to be the great witness for grace.

Paul says the same to the Galatians, sealing the point: "Abraham 'believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness'... so then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith" (Galatians 3:6-9). The family of Abraham is not defined by blood or by ritual. It is defined by faith, and it always was. The writer of Hebrews stands in the same line: Abraham "was as good as dead," and yet from that one man, "and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven" (Hebrews 11:12). The God of Abraham specializes in bringing life out of what is finished.

And the point of the whole chapter is not finally Abraham. It is the God Abraham trusted, "who gives life to the dead" (Romans 4:17). That God did not stay in Genesis. He walked out of a tomb outside Jerusalem, and Paul says the resurrection is the very ground of our being counted righteous: Jesus was "raised for our justification" (Romans 4:25). Read that verse with care, because Paul ties the two events together: Christ was "delivered up for our trespasses" — the cross deals with the debt — "and raised for our justification" — the empty tomb is God's public receipt that the debt is paid and the verdict stands. So the faith that saves you is not faith in your faith. It is not confidence in your sincerity or your track record or your religious badge. It is Abraham's faith aimed at Abraham's God, now revealed in the risen Christ — trust in the One who calls into being the things that are not, including, most impossibly, a righteousness for the ungodly.

This is where the chapter finally rests, and it is meant to hold a frightened conscience. If your acceptance before God depended on the quality of your believing, you would be back to works under a new name, forever taking your own spiritual temperature. But Abraham's faith was not impressive. It staggered. He laughed. He tried to arrange the promise himself through Hagar. The strength was never in the faith. It was in the God the faith laid hold of. A weak faith in a strong Savior saves; a strong faith in anything else does not. Rest your hope not on the firmness of your grip but on the One you are gripping.

- **A. Faith is not the achievement** — The moment we make faith the new work we perform to earn God, we have lost the chapter. Faith is the empty hand that receives, not the full hand that pays.
- **B. Raised for our justification** — Abraham believed the God who raises the dead; we believe the God who raised his Son. The empty tomb is the proof that the ledger is settled and the ungodly are counted righteous.

Counted righteous before he worked.

## Peace With God: Justified by Faith in the Second Adam (Romans 5:1-21)
*What we gain the moment we are justified, and why grace runs deeper than ruin*

**Text:** Romans 5:1-21 · **Supporting:** Genesis 3:17-19 · Isaiah 53:6 · 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 · Colossians 1:20 · John 3:16

Paul has finished the argument. The whole world guilty, Christ set forth as propitiation, the ungodly counted righteous by faith like Abraham. Now, for the first time in the letter, he turns from the courtroom to the household. He has told us what God has done. Now he tells us what we have — right now, today, as a settled possession. And the first word out of his mouth is the word the human race has been chasing since it was cast out of the garden. Peace. Not a truce. Not a ceasefire we must keep renewing. Peace with God, granted, held, secured.

The verdict of justification is not the end of Paul's good news. It is the door into it.

### I. Peace, Access, and Hope Through Justification (Romans 5:1-11)

"Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1). The verb is settled — *we have been justified*, done, complete. And on that foundation, three gifts. Peace with God. "Access by faith into this grace in which we stand" (Romans 5:2). And "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God." Once we were "haters of God" back in Romans 1:30; now we stand in his grace with the door held open. That is the reversal the whole letter was driving toward.

Then Paul does something the modern heart does not expect. He says suffering is not the enemy of this hope but its workshop. "We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us" (Romans 5:3-5). The word behind endurance is *hypomonē* — not gritted teeth but the capacity to remain under a weight without collapsing, because you know the One who holds you. Watch the chain: suffering, endurance, character, hope. Our culture treats suffering as the interruption of the good life, the thing to be medicated and escaped. Paul treats it as the forge where hope is hammered into something that will not bend when the light fails. He does not promise that suffering feels good. He promises that in the hands of God it is never wasted, and that is a different and far sturdier comfort than escape.

And Paul grounds all of it in the timing of the cross, which is the measure of the love. "For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly" (Romans 5:6). He drives it home: "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). Not after we cleaned up. Not once we came halfway. While we were still sinners — still enemies (Romans 5:10). Isaiah had said it: "the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). The love of God is not a response to our loveliness. It is love aimed at enemies, proven by a cross we did not deserve.

- **A. Peace as possession, not mood** — This peace is not a feeling you manufacture on a calm morning. It is an objective standing before God, secured by Christ, true on your worst day.
- **B. Love proven in the timing** — God did not wait for us to be worth dying for. Christ died while we were still sinners. The proof of the love is written into the moment it came.

### II. One Man's Trespass, One Man's Obedience (Romans 5:12-21)

Now Paul reaches all the way back to the beginning of the human story, because he refuses to start at the proximate cause. "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). One man, Adam, and a whole race under sin and death. When God said, "cursed is the ground because of you... you are dust, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:17-19), the sentence did not stop with Adam. It ran down every generation, into every grave, into yours and mine.

But Paul introduces Adam only to set up his opposite. Adam "was a type of the one who was to come" (Romans 5:14). There are, in the end, only two men in this chapter, and every human being is standing behind one of them. Paul builds the parallel and then breaks it open with a repeated phrase — *much more*. "But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many" (Romans 5:15). The second Adam does not merely undo the first. He overpays. Where Adam brought condemnation, Christ brings "justification and life" (Romans 5:18). "For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19). Paul had said the same to Corinth: "as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:21-22).

Then the line that towers over the chapter. "Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more" (Romans 5:20). Not merely matched. *Abounded all the more* — the grace runs past the ruin, deeper than the fall, wider than the wreckage. Sin reigned in death; grace now reigns "through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 5:21).

- **A. Two men, two humanities** — You are in Adam or you are in Christ. There is no third column. Your standing before God is decided by which man you are joined to.
- **B. Grace overflows the ruin** — Christ does not restore us to a neutral zero. Where sin increased, grace abounded more. The second Adam gives more than the first Adam lost.

### III. Standing in Grace in a Post-Christian Culture

Turn it on us, because our age has a settled and confident answer to Romans 5, and it is the exact opposite of Paul's. The modern West does not believe in one man's trespass, and it does not think it needs one man's obedience. It believes human beings are basically good and improvable by education and effort, that the trouble is out there in bad systems and never in here in a fallen heart, that with enough progress we will save ourselves. And I have preached a softened version of that same lie from inside the church — flattered the congregation that our real problem is our circumstances, never our sin, and offered a Christ who assists our self-improvement rather than one who died for our enmity.

The 1930s in Germany are the argument's black witness. A civilized, educated, church-going nation — the land of Luther, of Bach, of the university — persuaded itself of human goodness and national destiny, and within a decade it built the machinery of the death camps. When Adolf Eichmann, the administrator of the transports to Auschwitz, was tried in Jerusalem in 1961, the philosopher Hannah Arendt went expecting to find a monster and instead found a mediocre bureaucrat — a man who followed orders, filled out forms, sought promotion, and never grasped the enormity of what he had done. She called it the banality of evil. The horror, she saw, was not a fiend. It was a clerk. That is Romans 5:12 confirmed in the most literate century in history: death spread to all, because all sinned, and the polished heart is not the exception. It is the example. The doctrine of one man's trespass is not medieval gloom. It is the only honest account of the twentieth century, and of your Tuesday afternoon.

Someone will object that it is unjust to be counted a sinner in Adam, condemned for another man's act. Grant the objection its full weight — it is the sharpest one raised against this chapter. But then turn it, because the same logic that stumbles at Adam is the only logic that can save you in Christ. If you refuse to be reckoned guilty through the representative act of one man, you must also refuse to be reckoned righteous through the representative act of one man. The very principle you resent in Adam is the principle that rescues you in Christ. Federal representation is not a bug in the system. It is the mechanism of the gospel. You went down in a man; you can only come up in a Man.

But the doctrine is not finally about Adam. It is about the second Adam, and it ends not in dust but in glory. "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3:16). Through his cross God was "making peace by the blood of his cross" (Colossians 1:20) — the very peace Romans 5 opens with. So the question this chapter presses is simple and total. Which man are you standing behind? Because if it is Adam, the ledger is trespass, condemnation, death, and you inherit all of it. And if it is Christ, the ledger is obedience, justification, life — and grace that does not merely cover the ruin but abounds past it, all the way to the glory of God.

And this is where Romans 5 leaves the believer to stand. Not on a truce that must be renegotiated after every failure, but on peace with God secured by a Man who cannot fail. Your standing does not rest on your grip on Christ; it rests on his representative obedience credited to you, on grace that abounded past your ruin before you were born to commit it. The peace was made at the cross, in his blood, while you were still an enemy. It does not depend on your mood, your streak, or your worst Tuesday. It depends on which man you are in.

- **A. The flattering lie fails the test** — Every account of human nature that denies one man's trespass has to explain the ovens and the gulag, and it cannot. Paul can.
- **B. In Christ, grace overpays** — To be joined to the second Adam is to receive more than the first Adam lost. Not a repair. A superabundance. Peace with God that nothing can undo.

Where sin increased, grace abounded more.

## Dead to Sin, Alive to God: The End of Grace as a Loophole (Romans 6:1-23)
*Why the freed slave keeps returning to the auction block, and the death that ends it*

**Text:** Romans 6:1-23 · **Supporting:** Colossians 3:3 · Galatians 2:20 · Titus 2:11-12 · 1 Peter 2:24 · Ephesians 2:10

You can be forgiven and still be a slave. That is the wound Paul is pressing here, and it is the wound most of us are still nursing on a Tuesday afternoon — the sin we confessed on Sunday, met again on Monday, and made peace with by Wednesday, telling ourselves grace will cover it. It always does. That is exactly the problem Paul saw coming. Grace that covers everything can become the permission to do anything, and a man can spend his whole life at the foot of the cross and never once leave the auction block he was bought off of. Our post-Christian culture has its own version of this bargain, and it is everywhere. Forgiveness without repentance. Acceptance without change. The self affirmed exactly as it is, with no summons to become anything else. And the church, wanting to be liked, has too often borrowed the terms. So Paul asks the question that exposes us before we can hide. Not "may we sin." He knows we do. The question underneath is darker: why would a dead man want to.

### I. The Question Grace Provokes and the Death That Answers It (Romans 6:1-11)

Paul has just finished five chapters proving that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. And he knows precisely what the human heart does with that sentence. It reaches for the loophole. "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?" (Romans 6:1). The Greek is *epimenōmen* — to remain in, to persist, to make your home there. Not the stumble. The residence. Paul is not asking whether the justified man will fall. He is asking whether the justified man will move back in.

The question is not a straw man Paul invents to knock down. It is the oldest objection to grace, and it is a serious one. If God's love is not earned and cannot be forfeited, if the acquittal is total and the debt already paid, then what possible motive remains to say no to the thing you want. The moralist says the motive is fear of punishment. The legalist says the motive is fear of losing your standing. Paul removes both fears in chapter five and then turns, in chapter six, to give a motive neither of them could imagine. Not fear. Death. You do not refuse sin because you are afraid of losing grace. You refuse it because the you that wanted it has been buried.

His answer is the strongest negation in his vocabulary. *Mē genoito.* "By no means. How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). The whole argument turns on a death that has already happened. Not a death we are working toward. A death that is behind us. "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?" (Romans 6:3). The word *baptizō* buried a man in the water and raised him, and Paul reads the whole gospel into that going-under. We were buried with him. We were united with him in a death like his. And union runs both directions — "if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his" (Romans 6:5).

- **A. The old self was crucified, not counseled.** "We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin" (Romans 6:6). The old man is not being managed, disciplined, improved. He is executed. This is why Paul later writes to the Colossians, "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3). The freed man's problem is not that he lacks freedom. It is that he keeps forgetting he has it.
- **B. Reckon what is already true.** "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" (Romans 6:11). *Logizomai* — to reckon, to count as fact, the same word Paul used of Abraham's faith being counted as righteousness. This is not pretending. It is accounting. You do not make yourself dead to sin by trying. You count yourself dead because Christ made it so, and then you live from the ledger God has already closed.

### II. Which Slavery, Not Whether Slavery (Romans 6:12-23)

Here is where Paul refuses the sentimental version of freedom. He does not tell the Roman Christians they are now their own masters, self-directed, finally free to be themselves. He tells them they have changed owners. "Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?" (Romans 6:16). The question was never whether you would serve. The question is whom.

"Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions" (Romans 6:12). *Basileuō* — to reign, to hold the throne. Sin wants the crown back. And the freed slave, mysteriously, keeps offering it. So Paul commands the offering to go the other way: present "your members to God as instruments for righteousness" (Romans 6:13). The verb is the same one used for laying a sacrifice on the altar. Every morning is a presentation. You lay yourself down before something. The only question is what.

Notice the honesty in the word Paul chooses. He does not pretend the freed man has no master. The modern gospel of self-ownership — you belong to yourself, you answer to no one, you are the author of your own meaning — is a slavery Paul saw straight through two thousand years ago. There is no neutral ground where a person governs himself. The self that thinks it is free is simply obeying passions it did not choose and cannot control, and calling the obedience freedom. Paul's word for the alternative is not autonomy. It is a better ownership. "But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed" (Romans 6:17). From the heart. Not dragged. Not coerced. The mark of the new master is that the slave obeys him gladly.

- **A. Grace does not weaken the command; it grounds it.** "For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace" (Romans 6:14). Notice what he does not say. He does not say grace lowers the bar. He says grace breaks the dominion. This is why Titus can write that "the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions" (Titus 2:11-12). Grace is not the anesthetic that lets us keep sinning without pain. Grace is the trainer that drills us out of it. And Peter grounds the whole thing in the cross itself: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness" (1 Peter 2:24).
- **B. The two wages.** Paul ends with an accounting no one can argue with. "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). *Opsōnia* — a soldier's wages, what you earn, what is owed. Sin pays what it owes, and it always pays in full. Grace does not pay wages at all. It gives a gift. One column you earn. The other you could never earn. And a man who understands that he was bought does not go back to selling himself for what he was rescued from.

### III. Living Well When Grace Has Become a Loophole

I have preached grace as a loophole. Not in those words — no one preaches it in those words. I have preached it in the softer, kinder, more devastating form, where the altar call assumes the sin and the sermon assumes the return, where forgiveness is offered so cheaply and so often that the congregation learns, correctly, that nothing is expected to change. Dietrich Bonhoeffer named this in 1937, in *The Cost of Discipleship*, and the German church did not want to hear it any more than the American church does. He called it cheap grace — "the grace we bestow on ourselves," grace as a principle, forgiveness without repentance, the cross without discipleship. Bonhoeffer said cheap grace is the deadliest enemy of the church, and he was not describing the world outside the walls. He was describing us inside them. He wrote it seven years before the Nazis hanged him for costly grace. He knew the difference in his own body.

We have made grace the reason nothing changes. Paul made it the reason everything must. The difference between those two gospels is the difference between a man visiting his own grave and a man living in it. You died. That is not a metaphor you are asked to feel. It is a fact you are asked to count. And the crucified and risen Christ is not merely the one who forgives your slavery — he is the one whose death ended it and whose resurrection is the life you now live from. "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). We are his workmanship, "created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:10). The freedom was never freedom to sin. It was freedom from having to.

- **A. Stop asking what you can get away with.** That question is the question of a slave who does not yet believe he was freed. The dead do not ask it. Present yourself in the morning — not to the thing that owns nothing of you now, but to the God who owns all of you by blood.
- **B. Count before you fight.** The order in Romans 6 is reckon, then present, then obey. Most of us reverse it — we fight, then fail, then wonder if grace was real. Paul says the fighting flows from the reckoning. You do not battle sin to become dead to it. You battle it because you already are.

You died. Now live like it.

## The War the Law Could Not Win: Why the Good Command Cannot Save You (Romans 7:1-25)
*The holy law, the exposed sin, and the cry the rulebook was never able to answer*

**Text:** Romans 7:1-25 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:24 · Romans 3:20 · Exodus 20:17 · Psalm 51:5 · Galatians 5:17

Everyone I have ever counseled who was drowning in shame believed the same lie: that trying harder was the way out. That if they could just want the good enough, discipline the flesh enough, memorize the command enough, the war inside them would end in victory. Paul is about to take that hope apart. Not because the command is bad — he will insist, three times, that it is holy and good — but because the command was never a rescue. It was a diagnosis. And a man can memorize his diagnosis until he can recite it in his sleep and still die of the disease. Romans 7 is the chapter where the most sincere Christian discovers that his sincerity is not the answer, and that the very thing he was leaning on to save him has been quietly holding him under.

Our culture has traded the old rulebook for new ones, but it has not escaped the mechanism Paul is describing. The wellness regimen, the productivity system, the moral cause you signed onto to prove you are one of the good ones — each promises that the right discipline, followed with enough rigor, will finally make you whole. Each delivers the same verdict Paul is about to render. You will fall short of the standard you set for yourself, and the standard will not help you rise. It will only tell you how far you have fallen. That is not a flaw in the standard. That is what a standard is for.

### I. Released From the Law to Belong to Another (Romans 7:1-6)

Paul opens with a picture from the marriage bond, because the Romans knew it in their bones. "A married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage" (Romans 7:2). Death dissolves the bond. And then he turns it: "you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God" (Romans 7:4). The point is not that the law was cruel. The point is that we were bound to it as to a first husband who could command everything and empower nothing, and Christ's death ended that marriage so we could belong to a husband who does both.

"For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (Romans 7:5). This is the sentence that unsettles the moral man. The law did not neutralize the passions. It aroused them. Tell a man where the fence is, and something in him wants to climb it precisely because it is there.

- **A. The law binds until death breaks the bond.** Paul had already told the Galatians the law's true office: "the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith" (Galatians 3:24). *Paidagōgos* — not the teacher, but the household slave who walked the child to the teacher. The law was never the destination. It was the escort to the door.
- **B. We now serve in the new way of the Spirit.** "We serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (Romans 7:6). The written code — *gramma*, the letter carved in stone — could tell you the road and never move your feet. The war the moral man keeps losing is the war of trying to obey a husband who is dead.

### II. The Holy Law and the Sin It Exposes (Romans 7:7-25)

Now Paul defends the law against the very suspicion he has raised. "What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means. Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet'" (Romans 7:7). He reaches all the way back to the tenth word from Sinai — "You shall not covet" (Exodus 20:17) — the one commandment that indicts not the hand but the heart, the one no external conformity can satisfy. And the moment the command named the desire, the desire woke up. "But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness" (Romans 7:8).

This is the whole function Paul stated back in chapter three: "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (Romans 3:20). The mirror does not clean the face. It shows the dirt. And then Paul says the thing that has kept theologians arguing for centuries and keeps ordinary believers weeping in recognition: "For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" (Romans 7:15). "For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out" (Romans 7:18). The war is not between a man and his ignorance. He knows the good. He wants the good. And he cannot do it.

Read that slowly, because it undoes the whole self-help premise the modern West is built on. We are told the problem is a knowledge gap — if people just knew better, they would do better — or a willpower gap, that we lack the discipline to close the distance between our values and our lives. Paul says the gap is neither. He knows the good perfectly. He wants it genuinely. And still, reliably, he does the thing he hates. There is a saboteur living in the very house of the will, and no amount of information reaches it and no amount of resolve overpowers it. "So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand" (Romans 7:21). Close at hand. Not out in the culture. Not in the other tribe. In the marrow of the man who wants to be good.

- **A. The law is holy; the sin is the murderer.** "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good" (Romans 7:12). Paul will not let the failure indict the command. The command is a scalpel, not a wound. The murderer is sin, which "deceived me and through it killed me" (Romans 7:11). Every generation looks for a rulebook that will make it good, and every generation discovers the rulebook can only make it guilty.
- **B. The war is real, and the flesh is set against the Spirit.** "For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do" (Galatians 5:17). David knew the root ran deeper than any single act: "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me" (Psalm 51:5). The problem is not that we lack a good enough rule. The problem is in the marrow, and no rule reaches marrow.

### III. Living Well When You Have Tried Everything and It Was Not Enough

I have been the man who thought discipline would deliver him. I have stood in a pulpit and preached a victory I had not won that week, and then driven home and done the very thing I had just condemned, and hated myself the whole way. That is not a confession that makes me interesting. It is Romans 7, and if you have never lived in this chapter you have not yet taken the law seriously enough to be crushed by it. Martin Luther lived here for years before 1517. He was a monk who confessed his sins for hours, wore his confessor out, punished his body, and could not find peace, because the harder he tried to love God the more he found he resented the God who demanded what he could not give. His breakthrough was not a better technique. It was the discovery that the righteousness God required, God provided. The law drove Luther to the end of himself, and the end of himself was the beginning of grace.

That is the mercy hidden inside the misery of this chapter. The law is doing exactly what it was sent to do. It is not failing when it leaves you exhausted and guilty. It is succeeding. It is walking you, like a guardian slave, to the only door that opens. Paul does not end Romans 7 with a strategy. He ends it with a scream and then a name. "Wretched man that I am. Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 7:24-25). The deliverer is not a program. He is a person. And the war the law could never win, Christ won on a cross the law itself pronounced the sentence for.

This is why the therapeutic culture, for all its kindness, cannot finally reach the place Paul is describing. It can help you set a boundary and name a pattern and quiet a symptom, and it should be honored for the good it does. But it works entirely inside the self — better management of the will, better understanding of the wound — and the whole burden of Romans 7 is that the self is the thing that has failed. You cannot lift yourself off the ground by pulling on your own arms. The deliverance the man in this chapter needs cannot come from inside the man, because inside the man is precisely where the war is lost. It has to come from outside. It has to come from someone who is not himself a casualty of the same war. There is exactly one such person, and Paul names him, and the whole letter has been building to the naming.

- **A. Stop asking the law to do what only Christ can.** The rulebook was never the rescue. When you have exhausted your willpower, you have not failed the assignment. You have finished it. The exhaustion is the escort.
- **B. Let the cry become the confession.** The question "who will deliver me" is not despair when it ends where Paul ends it. It is the last honest thing a striving man says before he finally lets himself be saved.

Who will deliver me from this body.

## No Condemnation, No Separation: The Two Walls That Hold the Christian (Romans 8:1-39)
*The verdict behind you, the glory ahead of you, and the love that cannot be pried loose*

**Text:** Romans 8:1-39 · **Supporting:** Romans 5:1 · Galatians 4:6 · Ephesians 1:13-14 · John 10:28 · Philippians 1:6
